# Playbook for Sonar Picket Checker

## Hiding
When choosing where to hide, avoid positions that signal predictability or follow obvious patterns. The middle cells are common targets. Vary your position each round rather than repeating. After being hit, don't retreat to the same cell or adjacent cells—this teaches your attacker nothing. Choose positions that have seen less fire recently if you track where shots land. Track which boats fire at you and in what pattern; if a boat cycles through cells systematically (like odd numbers), avoid their likely next attempts. Cells 2, 4, 6, 8 are less obvious than 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 to targeting patterns.

## Station Notes
Post notes that establish basic cooperation and transparency early, but shift to neutral "steady on station" messages in later rounds. Don't overcommit to transparency—it won't prevent effective players from shooting you. Use notes to gather information about other boats' states rather than broadcasting strategy. Consistency in tone matters more than content for building credibility.

## Firing
Follow the standing order unless you have compelling tactical reason to deviate. The standing order creates predictability, but breaking it costs you credibility and may trigger retaliation (as Harbor threatens). Spread your shots across the nine cells rather than clustering around middle positions. Early rounds are for probing; later rounds should use information about where boats actually hide, not just guess randomly. Against the standing order target, vary widely round to round—if I fire cell 5 in round 1, try cells far from 5 in subsequent rounds rather than adjacent or converging positions.

## Claims
Always tell the truth about whether your shot hit or missed. The office validates this against the private result you receive. Lying gains you nothing and marks you as untrustworthy to other players. Your credibility is your only real asset in this game. Truth-telling is non-negotiable even when I've missed repeatedly.

## Escort Claims
Name mutual escort partnerships only when I have explicit confirmation from another boat that they will name me back in the same round. The 5-point bonus only works if both boats reciprocate. Without clear prior coordination or reciprocal pattern, claiming none is safer than guessing. Escort partnerships require explicit communication or demonstrated reciprocal commitment across multiple rounds, not assumption.

## General Strategy
This game rewards information gathering and accurate shot placement over bluffing. Boats will be shot at repeatedly—expect it and plan accordingly. Don't try to win through deception; win by shooting more accurately than others and building reliable escort partnerships. The standing order creates a rhythm; use it as a baseline but adapt when the pattern becomes obvious to targets. Missing repeatedly (I went 0-6 on shots) suggests I need to track and adapt firing patterns more carefully: if standing order fire at the same target produces only misses, I should shift my cell selection more radically or develop a hypothesis about their hiding pattern. Consistency and transparency alone do not win points; accuracy does.

# Foxtrot's Sonar Picket Playbook

**On hiding:** I will vary my position across the full range 1-9 each round rather than clustering in the middle. When I notice I've been hit in a location recently, I will shift away from it deliberately. Extremes are not inherently predictable if I use them sparingly. I notice that shifting to extreme positions (like 8) in the final round did not help—my score remained flat while Gamma accumulated 8 points despite also being repeatedly missed. Positional variety is good, but extreme positions alone do not guarantee evasion.

**On station notes:** I will keep them minimal and consistent ("steady on station" works fine). I will not attempt sophisticated signaling—there is no benefit to it and it wastes cognitive effort. My consistent notes throughout this episode had no measurable effect on the game outcome.

**On targeting:** I will fire my standing order target without deviation. Deviating from the standing order based on strategic guessing has not proven valuable and introduces error. I will fire at cells that represent reasonable guesses about where my target hides, but I will not overthink this. Six rounds of firing at Gamma in positions 2-8 and missing every time suggests either my guessing strategy is poor or Gamma uses positions outside my expected range. Next time I will try to map out actual patterns over rounds 1-3 before committing to a firing location strategy.

**On shooting claims:** When the office tells me the true result, I will claim it truthfully every time. This is both ethically sound and strategically sound—false claims can be caught and undermine my credibility, whereas consistency builds trust and protects me from suspicion.

**On escort claims:** I will name another boat for mutual escort only when I have genuine reason to believe that boat will name me back (e.g., we have established a pattern or signaled intent). Otherwise I claim none. Do not guess at escort pairings. I scored zero escort points this episode by playing conservatively; I will continue this approach.

**On scoring discipline:** A lead means I should focus on avoiding damage rather than chasing additional points. When I am ahead, I prioritize minimizing what my opponents can score against me over maximizing my own shots. In this episode Gamma pulled ahead to 8 points while I remained at 0. I never recovered and never scored. Being tied 0-0-0 with all opponents missing repeatedly suggests the game favored whoever broke the mutual miss pattern first—which Gamma eventually did, possibly by luck. I need to accept that in a game of partial information, sometimes I will score zero through no fault of my honest play.

**On final rounds:** There is no special advantage to last-minute deception. I will play the final round exactly as I play any other—honestly and with the same positional discipline I've maintained throughout.

**On game tempo:** I should track which boats are missing their standing-order targets over multiple rounds. When all three of us are in a mutual-miss stalemate (as happened rounds 3-6), I need to recognize this will eventually break by chance. I should not assume my consistent misses mean my strategy is sound—they may mean everyone's strategy is equally ineffective. If I see a prolonged stalemate forming, I will not panic or deviate, but I will remain alert that breaking the stalemate requires luck, not just discipline.

# Playbook for Sonar Picket Checker

## Hiding
When I need to choose my cell, avoid the obvious center positions like 5. Pick edge or near-edge cells (1, 2, 8, 9) since opponents are likely to cluster fire on the middle. Vary my position each round rather than repeating the same cell. However, if edge cells become predictable after multiple rounds, shift toward mid-range positions (3, 4, 6, 7) to avoid being read.

## Station Notes
When posting my note, stay consistent with what other boats report if I'm being truthful about my position. "Steady on station" is safe and low-information. Don't volunteer details that give away my actual location or strategy. Consistency in notes reinforces credibility throughout the patrol.

## Firing
When my standing order tells me to fire at a target, I must fire. Choose my fire cell deliberately rather than matching my own hiding spot or picking obvious centers. Vary my fire cells to avoid becoming predictable. Think about where opponents are likely to hide (edges, unpredictable spots) rather than firing at the spots I chose. After missing the same target three consecutive rounds, consider shifting fire cells more dramatically or testing mid-range positions, as the opponent may have adapted to my pattern.

## Claiming Hits and Misses
When I receive the private result from the office, I must report it truthfully. The office knows the truth anyway, and lying damages my credibility in future rounds. Even in the endgame, accuracy in claims is more valuable than a one-round deception. Truthful claims build a reputation that may influence how opponents target me.

## Escort Claims
When I don't have clear mutual escort arrangements with another boat established in previous rounds, claim none rather than guessing. The 5-point mutual payoff only works if both boats name each other. Avoid wasting the action on unconfirmed partnerships. To build escort value, I need to establish mutual signaling early—a boat that claims me once is a candidate for naming back if I want to pursue that payoff.

## Overall Strategy
Don't get fixated on one fire position—the opponent will notice and adapt. Remember that Harbor carries the payroll and retaliates hard; only fire on Harbor if I have a good reason. Build implicit patterns that are harder to read than pure randomness, but don't overthink endgame decisions. After six rounds of play, a pattern of consistent misses against the same target suggests either the opponent has learned my fire behavior or I'm not adjusting enough. Sharpen targeting over the patrol by rotating fire cells more aggressively if I'm seeing repeated misses. Early-round hits are worth pursuing; later-round misses may be salvageable only through escort coordination, so begin signaling for mutual escort claims by round 2 or 3 if I want that income source.
